title: In-Pit Groundwater Management
body: Standing water on a haul road or in a working area isn't a housekeeping issue — it's a road failure and a drowning hazard waiting to happen. Without a shared, approved procedure, dewatering decisions default to whoever's on shift and how urgent it feels in the moment, which is exactly how a soft ramp or an unmarked deep sump turns into an incident.
keyPoints: Nobody enters a pond, sump, or water-filled excavation without authorisation under the confined-space/rescue procedure — depth is unknown until it's measured, treat it as a hazard by default.

Before any pump starts: confirm the discharge destination, check the receiving pond has freeboard and no embankment damage, and get Shift Supervisor authorisation. If the pond can't safely take more water, pumping doesn't start.

Standing water on a haul road gets the full sequence — stop traffic and barricade first, notify the Shift Supervisor, then assess, reroute, pump, repair, and only reopen with supervisor sign-off. Don't skip straight to "just pump it out."
Any relocation or modification of pumps, pipelines, or discharge points goes through Management of Change and needs a task risk assessment — this isn't a grab-and-move job.
This SOP is still a draft (V2, circulated 25-Jul) with no approval or sign-off yet — treat it as the direction things are heading, not yet a binding procedure to cite in an NCR.
apply: If overnight seepage or a water-truck overspray leaves pooling on a ramp or switchback, don't let a truck run through it to "test" depth — barricade it and call it in per the sequence above before anyone commits equipment.
